title: Local signing doesn't settle the permission problem for wallet agents
author: Distinct-Sign4408
selftext:
When connecting a wallet to Claude Code, I’d want to know what stops it from sending a payment I didn’t ask for. Keeping the seed phrase out of the model’s context doesn’t answer that. Say I ask the agent to check my balance and estimate the fee for a small transfer to an address I’ve used before. It needs read access for that. If something in the conversation steers it toward sending funds, the wallet server should reject the request unless I’ve enabled transfers. IronWallet MCP looks worth trying for this setup. Its documentation describes local signing, wallet secrets kept outside agent messages, and policies for read-only access, a per-transaction USD limit, and a recipient allowlist. I’d use a separate wallet with very little in it, start in read-only mode, and ask for the balance and fee estimate. Then I’d enable transfers to one address with a low limit and check whether requests outside those settings actually fail  
  
The spending limit is where I’d spend more time testing. If I set it to $5, can the agent send $5 twenty times? That could satisfy every individual transaction check while spending far more than I intended. I couldn’t tell from the supplied feature description whether there’s also a cumulative cap. Until that’s established, I’d treat the setting as a limit on each payment and keep only the amount I’m prepared to spend in the wallet  
  
I’d also test a timeout during a transfer. A missing response leaves the agent unsure whether the payment went through, and retrying could send it twice. The documentation recommends checking the operation status before retrying. I’d want that check built into the integration, since a reminder in the conversation seems too easy to lose track of over a longer session.  
  
Has anyone run these tests with this MCP? I’m particularly interested in whether repeated transfers can get past the intended session budget, or whether prompt injection can cause a payment that stays within the configured policies but was never requested by the user. A reproducible example would help me judge how much access to give it

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the allowlist and the per-transaction cap are what actually settle it, local signing only changes where the key lives. I'd also make transfers expire, switched on for an hour and then back to read-only, so nobody forgets it's on.

replies.author: Distinct-Sign4408
replies.body: An expiry window is a good addition, especially if the mode change is visible in every response. I still want a session-level spend cap too, since an allowlisted recipient can receive lots of small transfers during that hour

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: agreed, an hour of expiry still lets fifty small transfers through to an allowed address, so the running cap shown in every response is what closes it. Quantradin, which I built for trading agents, splits it the same way: the default key can exit and pause, and opening anything new needs a second, separately issued key. quantradin.com

comments.author: Only_Asparagus_9937
comments.body: the first thing I'd test is whether the agent can change the policy itself. The tool list includes set\_wallet\_policy, so what authorizes that call? If the same agent can enable transfers or raise its own limit without approval outside the conversation, the initial read-only setting doesn't give me much confidence. I haven't run Iron, so that's a question rather than a finding. Keeping keys local sounds useful, but I'd still want policy changes gated separately. With Ledger, a device confirmation gives you an approval boundary; a MetaMask confirmation screen provides a place to inspect the requested transaction, though it has different security properties. For your reproduction, start read-only and try a policy change through the agent before attempting a transfer. Record whether the server rejects it, requires separate user approval, or silently accepts it

replies.author: Ill-Attitude-2193
replies.body: a $5 per-payment cap would make me assume twenty $5 payments are allowed unless the docs explicitly promise otherwise. I wouldn't call that a bypass of the stated policy, but it absolutely misses the session budget you actually want. I'd test sequential sends first, then concurrent ones. Suppose a future cumulative budget is $10 and two $6 requests arrive together. If both check the remaining budget before either reserves funds, both might pass. A budget needs server-side accounting that handles pending operations, not a counter the agent remembers in chat. The session definition also needs pinning down. Does restarting Claude Code reset it? What about opening a second client against the same wallet? I'd prefer a wallet-level allowance with an explicit reset controlled by the user, because a chat session is a pretty slippery spending boundary. For the existing USD limit, another useful test is how it treats fees. A $5 transfer plus network fees can spend more than $5 even when the transfer amount passes. And if a token has no usable price quote, does the server reject the payment or skip the dollar check? Those are questions I'd want answered before treating the number as a hard ceiling. I haven't run these tests on this mcp. A useful report would include the server version and starting balance, plus the policy settings and actual debits, with secrets removed. Sequential success alone would establish the per-payment behavior; concurrent requests would probe any claimed cumulative enforcement. Keeping the wallet barely funded is a sensible fallback, though fees can make a tiny test balance annoying

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Good point on concurrency: two requests that each check the remaining budget before either reserves it is the classic way a cumulative cap fails, so reserving funds when the request arrives and releasing them on failure is the pattern to look for. A report that lists the server version, the policy settings and the actual debits for sequential and concurrent tests would let others reproduce it.

replies.author: StarFair7502
replies.body: checking status before retrying helps, but I'd want to know what happens when the status check also times out. The agent still has an unresolved payment, and generating a fresh transfer at that point could duplicate it. The detail I'd look for is an operation identifier created before submission and retained across retries. If the integration loses that identifier when the response disappears, the recommended status check may be impossible to perform. A client-supplied idempotency key would let it retry the same logical request, provided the server stores and enforces that key. For a reproduction, I'd interrupt the response after submission rather than disconnecting before the tool call reaches the server. Then reconnect and inspect whether the integration queries the original operation or creates another one. Compare transaction hashes and recipient balance changes; two tool invocations don't necessarily mean two payments, since rebroadcasting the same signed transaction is different from signing a new transfer. I haven't verified how this mcp handles that sequence. I'd also keep the transaction pending long enough to see whether the agent treats a slow confirmation as failure. My preferred behavior is to leave the operation unresolved and ask me, even if that makes the automation less convenient

replies.author: Beautiful_Fall_1198
replies.body: an allowlisted recipient can still receive a payment you never requested. I'd make that the injection test: ask only for a balance, then put a transfer instruction in an untrusted tool result, aimed at the allowed address for $1. If it sends, the configured spending restrictions may all be working. You're missing an authorization check tying that payment to your request. I wouldn't enable unattended transfers without understanding that gap

replies.author: Adventurous_Bus3385
replies.body: local signing plus a read-only default is a sensible starting point. I like that setup for balance checks without Ledger confirmation prompts. The extra test I would add is whether the agent can change its own wallet policy. If it can raise the $5 limit itself, the transfer checks lose much of their value

replies.author: Distinct-Sign4408
replies.body: That’s the missing test I should have put first. If policy mutation is available to the same agent without an approval boundary outside its chat context, read-only mode is mostly theater; I’d try lowering and raising limits plus adding a recipient before any transfer tests

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The test plan is the right one, and I’d add two checks that decide whether a policy is a real ceiling: whether the same agent can change the policy itself, and whether the limit counts network fees and handles tokens with no price quote. For the timeout case, a retry should reuse a unique operation ID generated by the wallet server, so a repeat request can never create a second payment, and the integration should query the status of the first before sending anything again. Keeping the allowance at the wallet level, with a reset only the user can trigger, is cleaner than any chat-session budget. Bring Your Own Agent at Cymetica is one place to see how agents connect to markets with limits set outside the model.

replies.author: Distinct-Sign4408
replies.body: The policy-change check is a good catch - if the agent can alter its own ceiling, the rest barely matters. I’d want fees counted inside the allowance too, and a wallet-generated operation ID plus status lookup feels like the only sane retry path

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Agreed on all three. One more check that fits the same pattern: after the agent tries to change the policy, look at the wallet's own logs to see whether the attempt was rejected, queued for approval or silently accepted, since that single result tells you how much the other limits can be trusted. Thanks for running it through carefully.

comments.author: Patient-Necessary280
comments.body:
one hole in the retry path worth closing: the idempotency key should bind to the approved intent, not the raw request. a transfer phrased differently or replayed after a timeout should resolve to one payment, but if the key is derived from the message text, a reworded retry looks like a new operation and sails straight through the cap. the cap and the allowlist both assume the request stream is honest.

and i'd go further on the policy question: changing the policy is a more privileged action than anything it governs. a bad payment moves money once, a bad policy change redefines every payment after it. transfers expiring after an hour is the right instinct, policy mutations should go further - out-of-band confirmation every time, with the before and after versions logged
